No, I kept the horse for myself.
Timur found a stable for me nearby.
Here, these are my personal savings.

Elena Pavlovna, we found the money!
We collected almost the entire sum.
Lena, what happened just now?
They replied to me from the German clinic.
The operation will be twice as expensive.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: For a week we will manage somehow by ourselves.
We are all true professionals, after all.
In the evening we will hold our elections.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'with / from', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: His condition is stable but serious.
Thank goodness, this is treatable now.
An urgent operation in Germany is needed.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'your (informal)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The waiters are carrying your fish back.
First I will get checked for rabies.
I got acquainted with your nephew.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'father' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: But after all, he is my father.
I built a hotel in Saint Petersburg.

examples.text: Я просто хотел спросить про отца.
examples.trans: I just wanted to ask about your father.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I do not have that kind of money.
Money is not a problem, right, Mom?
There is no need to sell anything right now.

meanings.en: to get along, to be on good terms
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'got along', paired with 'поладить'.

examples.text: Мы с твоим отцом не ладили.
examples.trans: Your father and I did not get along.
He and I get along wonderfully.

examples.text: Эдуард Владимирович, я на минуточку. Я спасла монастырь!
examples.trans: Eduard Vladimirovich, I'll only be a minute. I saved the monastery!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: His condition is stable but serious.
But after all, he is my father.
He will definitely help us.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'man' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Where are you headed, young man?
But he is truly a good man.
A person's life depends on pieces of paper.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: But after all, he is my father.
He will definitely help us.
He is sidelined for about a week.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'really', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Viktor Petrovich will definitely recover soon.
For a week we will manage somehow by ourselves.
It is truly very hard for me right now.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('good').

examples.trans: I will also give you a good discount.
Listen, well done, you know how to bargain well.
The discounted fish went down well!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (informal)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Are you the boss in here now, or what?
You are a completely irresponsible cook.

examples.text: Михаил Джекович коня в карты выиграл.
examples.trans: Mikhail Jekovich won a horse at cards.

meanings.en: after all, still, all the same
meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'ё-таки').

examples.trans: Did you sell your horse after all?
He came after all.
Maybe we'll go after all?

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'дать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to sell', paired with 'продавать'.

examples.trans: I can sell my apartment.
There is no need to sell anything right now.
I am selling a thoroughbred horse!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'their own', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I can sell my apartment.
I do not treat my competitors.
Did you sell your horse after all?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'horse; knight (in chess)' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: That is it, candidate registration is already closed.

examples.text: Михаил Джекович коня в карты выиграл.
examples.trans: Mikhail Jekovich won a horse at cards.
Did the horse arrive to pay off an old debt?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'no', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I do not have that kind of money.
No, it did not work out again today.
No, one cannot do that at all.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: His condition is stable but serious.
Thank goodness, this is treatable now.
An urgent operation in Germany is needed.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to oneself', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Wow, that is quite a fine.
No, I kept the horse for myself.
I feel good.

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'left', paired with 'оставлять'.

examples.trans: I cannot leave him in the courtyard.
No, I kept the horse for myself.
I won't leave him on his own.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'stable' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Tell me, is this a hotel or a stable?
Timur found a stable for me nearby.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'далеко'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Timur found a stable for me nearby.
The apple does not fall far from the tree.
We live not far from the center.

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to find', paired with 'находить'.

examples.trans: I will hire a temporary chef.
Where will I find movers?
I found the phone.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'here, there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: They will cook him right with carrots.
Wow, that is quite a fine.
Where is that foolish animal right now?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, it (is)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: By estimates this costs a lot.
Actually, it is a big problem.
Wait, this is not a horse.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: But after all, he is my father.
My acquaintance runs a Tatar restaurant.
She herself is ashamed to hear that.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('personal').

examples.trans: Great, now you have voted fairly.
Here, these are my personal savings.
That's a personal question.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'бережение'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'savings' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Here, these are my personal savings.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть сбережение.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always savings.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'пасибо'). Common neuter noun meaning 'thank you' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Thank you all for your trust!
Thank you, guys, let us work now.
Thank you for the pleasant company.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Lyova has a bad leg sprain.
He is sidelined for about a week.
Let us hold fair elections here.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('immense').

examples.trans: Thank you so very much, dear guys.
Our chances are huge.
Thank you so much!

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'рогой'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('dear').

examples.trans: By estimates this costs a lot.
Dear friend, well, how was your flight?
Forgive me, please, dear friend.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'guys, team' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Thank you, guys, let us work now.
Thank you so very much, dear guys.
Guys, where are you?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'money' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Money is not a problem, right, Mom?
We are looking for money everywhere right now.
That kind of money for a small horse?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'обрать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to collect, to gather', paired with 'собирать'.

examples.trans: We collected almost the entire sum.
They can't raise the money.
Pack your things.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'almost', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Strange, why did he not call?
We collected almost the entire sum.

examples.text: Почему в жизни всё так несправедливо?
examples.trans: Why is everything in life so unfair?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'entire', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Do you have a conscience at all?
Who is my future daughter-in-law kissing?
Denis, you are simply a shameless nephew!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'умма'). Common feminine noun meaning 'sum' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: We collected almost the entire sum.
The sum is very large.
What amount?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: His condition is stable but serious.
Thank goodness, this is treatable now.
An urgent operation in Germany is needed.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what, that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Потому что она совсем не свежая.
examples.trans: Because it is not fresh at all.
Senya, what is wrong with you right now?
So we can have lunch.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: Thank goodness, this is treatable now.
There is no need to sell anything right now.
Quiet, there is no need to argue now.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лучиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'happened', paired with 'случаться'.

examples.trans: What happened?
Nothing will happen.

examples.text: Марина, я вам обещаю: со стеной ничего не случится.
examples.trans: Marina, I promise you: nothing will happen to the wall.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'ветить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'answered', paired with 'отвечать'.

examples.trans: They replied to me from the German clinic.
I have to answer.
Answer me!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'from/out of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The plane is not flying because of bad weather.
This is all because of your horse!
They replied to me from the German clinic.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'мецкий'). Relational adjective formed with the Slavic suffix '-ский' ('pertaining to'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('German').

examples.trans: They replied to me from the German clinic.
The car is German.
It's a German house.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'clinic, hospital' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: They replied to me from the German clinic.

examples.text: Девочка уже две недели лежит в областной клинике!
examples.trans: The girl has been lying in the regional clinic for two weeks already!

examples.text: Врач работает в новой детской клинике.
examples.trans: The doctor works at the new children's clinic.

meanings.note: International noun in '-ция' (from Latin '-tio'), feminine declension. Common feminine noun meaning 'operation' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: An urgent operation in Germany is needed.
Dad needs an operation in Germany.

examples.text: Операция будет в два раза дороже.
examples.trans: The operation will be twice as expensive.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'will be'.

examples.trans: A captain must always be fair.
I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank goodness, this is treatable now.
An urgent operation in Germany is needed.
Actually, it is a big problem.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian cardinal or ordinal numeral meaning 'two', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Fine, but take two crates.
We have two kinds of ballots.

examples.text: Операция будет в два раза дороже.
examples.trans: The operation will be twice as expensive.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'times' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: They will steal the whole kitchen under you.
Fyodor, I will sort this out without you.
He happens to need horsemeat right now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, near, with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank goodness, this is treatable now.
An urgent operation in Germany is needed.
I do not have that kind of money.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'very', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: On the other hand, he is a very thoroughbred pony.
It is truly very hard for me right now.
By the way, this is very tasty fish.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ложный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('complicated, difficult').

examples.trans: He has a very complicated case.
Look, there's nothing complicated.
That's a very difficult question.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лучай'). Common masculine noun meaning 'case' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Lena, what happened just now?
He has a very complicated case.
Take it, just in case.
